title: Long-lived, low-intervention nuclear power for remote sites

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a compact, transportable nuclear system that supplies useful electricity or heat at a difficult-to-access site for decades with little on-site intervention. Its defining capability would be sustained service across the operating lifecycle, including the equipment and support needed to keep delivering energy. A long-lived reactor core would be one component of that capability. DOE’s discussion of transportable microreactors for remote applications provides a relevant development basis, while the decades-long service objective remains hypothetical.

Proposed scope. The system would combine an extended fuel or core lifetime with dependable heat removal, controls, remote supervision, maintenance arrangements, security, and eventual removal or disposal. Low intervention would have to be defined through actual staffing, inspection, servicing, and emergency-response requirements. Radioisotope generators and fission microreactors should be assessed separately against explicit power, fuel, and service requirements. The supplied evidence does not document their technical comparison or establish that either could meet the complete proposed specification.

significance.text: Achieving this capability could materially change energy provision at remote commercial or residential locations and military bases, applications identified in DOE’s microreactor discussion. The direct consequence would be a sustained local supply of electricity or useful heat with extended intervals between refueling. Reliable low-intervention service over decades would extend the development goals described in that source.

Conditional impact synthesis. At sites where fuel deliveries and maintenance visits are major logistical burdens, reducing those demands could improve continuity of service and make long-duration activity easier to sustain. Whether the system would lower total costs or enable additional activities would depend on site-specific demand, transport constraints, availability, staffing, security, and end-of-life arrangements. The supplied evidence does not quantify remote logistics costs or establish that fuel delivery and maintenance dominate costs at any particular site.

Impact boundary synthesis. Broad adoption would require evidence that the complete installation remains dependable and economically useful under its intended conditions. Transportability and extended core life alone cannot establish the required operating burden. The analogy to a power source that can simply be installed and left alone would therefore require explicit limits covering supervision, inspections, repairs, security response, and eventual recovery.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is the integration of extended nuclear energy production with a demonstrably low service burden throughout a remote installation’s life. DOE describes long core life, passive safety, operator requirements, and removal or replacement goals. Its article supplies only part of the basis for assessing the broader lifecycle objective. It does not establish decades of dependable operation with little intervention.

Proposed engineering barriers. Fuel integrity and heat removal would need to remain adequate over the claimed operating period, while controls and supporting equipment would need to tolerate aging and foreseeable operating disturbances. The assessment would need to determine which components require servicing or replacement, how faults are detected, and how the system reaches and maintains a safe condition when local intervention or remote communication is unavailable. These are proposed requirements for the concept. Their complete technical scope is not substantiated by the supplied article.

Proposed operational barriers. Remote supervision, physical security, maintenance access, and emergency response must be compatible with the claimed low-intervention service model. Removal, transport, and the ultimate disposition of the installation and its nuclear material also need workable arrangements. DOE’s stated removal and exchange goal leaves disposal questions open in this evidence record. A further challenge is establishing credible full-life performance when a field demonstration covers only part of a claimed multidecade lifetime.

current_state.text: In its February 26, 2021 article, DOE describes most microreactor designs as capable prospectively of producing 1–20 MW of thermal energy and lists operation for up to 10 years without refueling as a benefit. The output range is thermal output. Electrical delivery would require a separately specified conversion system and performance figure. Both the output range and refueling interval are presented as design characteristics or expected benefits. The article provides no demonstration of a system operating for 20–50 years without maintenance.

The DOE article connects compact, transportable microreactors with remote applications and discusses electricity and heat uses, passive safety, operator requirements, and removal or exchange. These statements establish relevant development goals. The supplied review identifies no operating record that demonstrates the complete decades-long, low-intervention capability. This evidence limitation leaves achievements elsewhere and subsequent developments unverified.

Evidence scope. According to the supplied review and source index, the retained DOE HTML article was complete and untruncated, with no recorded extraction issues. Its linked infographic and video were outside the inspected material. The article was retrieved on November 11, 2026, but its publication date remains February 26, 2021. The review’s freshness search record was empty, so the supplied material does not establish deployment status as of November 1, 2026 or developments through the later retrieval date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Operate a representative complete system at a remote site for a justified, service-relevant period. Independently measure delivered electricity and useful heat, availability, interruptions, degradation, refueling, planned and unplanned maintenance, and all on-site interventions. Document the actual staffing and remote oversight required, including inspections and responses to faults. Define the intended loads and environmental conditions before testing so the demonstrated service capability has clear boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Remote-site operation demonstrates measured energy service and intervention requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed lifetime substantiation. Support any longer service-life claim with an explicit evidence chain connecting field operation, component endurance testing, aging analysis, fuel-performance evidence, and uncertainty estimates. Explain how the method accounts for failure mechanisms that a shorter trial may miss. A service-relevant trial would establish performance over its observed duration. Claims extending beyond that duration would require a justified method of extrapolation.
completion_criteria.label: Service-life claims beyond trials substantiated through justified evidence-based extrapolation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed lifecycle and practical assessment. Independently assess security arrangements, maintenance and recovery logistics, total lifecycle cost, and end-of-life handling. Demonstrate removal or exchange where those actions form part of the service model, and establish credible arrangements for subsequent disposition. Specify which activities require specialist personnel, local access, or external infrastructure, and include their time and cost in the assessment.
completion_criteria.label: Independent lifecycle assessment accounts for practical support and disposition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and breadth. Make the evaluation methods, intervention records, performance data, and relevant operating assumptions available for independent assessment, with justified restrictions for sensitive information. Repeat representative evaluations across additional units or sites sufficient to test the intended deployment range. These are proposed criteria, with thresholds to be justified for the application. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within tested conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Accessible evaluation evidence and repeated trials establish demonstrated deployment breadth

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. NUC-02, Mass-produced fission plants with radically lower delivered cost, overlaps through manufacturing, deployment, and total system economics. Its stated focus is fleet-wide delivered cost, while NUC-10 focuses on long-duration service where access and logistics are unusually difficult. The roster supplies NUC-02’s title, so this boundary is an editorial interpretation of the supplied entries.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-06, Reactor structural materials that remain reliable under extreme neutron exposure, NUC-09, Very-high-burnup fuel with robust fission-product retention, and NUC-11, Durable materials and chemistry control for aggressive reactor coolants, address potential contributors to extended service life. Their relevance depends on the selected reactor design and operating conditions. Each concerns a narrower materials, fuel, or coolant capability, while NUC-10 requires integrated lifecycle performance.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-08, Broadly applicable passive shutdown and long-term reactor cooling, overlaps with maintaining safe conditions when intervention is delayed. NUC-12, Reliable, non-invasive, real-time three-dimensional reactor-core diagnosis, could contribute information for supervision and maintenance decisions. NUC-05, Practical remote verification of otherwise inaccessible operating reactors, concerns verification access and evidence about reactor operation. These titles describe complementary safety, diagnostic, and verification capabilities whose contribution to low-intervention operation would require separate demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-03, A scalable closed fuel cycle that consumes most long-lived actinides, and NUC-13, A fuel cycle with substantially stronger built-in proliferation resistance, overlap with fuel management and eventual material disposition. NUC-10 would need credible fuel and end-of-life arrangements, but its service objective does not itself establish actinide consumption or stronger proliferation resistance.

Roster-based synthesis. NUC-01, A self-sustaining, net-electric fusion power plant, and NUC-07, Net-electric fusion using a low-neutron fuel cycle, concern distinct energy-generation breakthroughs. Successful fusion systems might eventually be assessed for remote service, but those titles alone establish no compactness, transportability, or low-intervention capability. NUC-04, High-power nuclear propulsion for routine deep-space missions, shares the challenge of nuclear operation under difficult access conditions and adds propulsion-specific requirements. Its mission objective remains distinct from supplying electricity or heat to remote sites.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish deployment status or subsequent achievements as of November 2026.

The intended service lifetime, delivered electrical or heat output, allowable intervention frequency, and acceptable availability remain unspecified. The 20–50-year comparison is not an adopted performance threshold.
Evidence for the complete fuel-integrity, security, remote-supervision, maintenance, and disposal requirements remains incomplete.

The supplied material does not document the technical comparison between radioisotope generators and fission microreactors or establish which architecture could meet the proposed service requirements.
A justified method for substantiating full service life from shorter-duration demonstrations remains to be defined.
Site-specific lifecycle economics, staffing requirements, security arrangements, and end-of-life feasibility remain unverified.
Detailed overlap with other roster concepts remains provisional because their full records were not supplied.

brief.title: Decades of remote nuclear power with few service visits
possible: People living or working far from easy transport links could get dependable electricity or useful heat for decades from a compact nuclear system. It would need little work on site, with support arrangements covering everything from routine operation to eventual removal.
why: Remote communities, businesses and military bases could sustain their activities with fewer refueling and maintenance visits. Where those visits are difficult, reducing them could help keep energy supplies running.

sources.who: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy
sources.showed: The department describes microreactors, compact nuclear reactors designed for transport, as potential sources of electricity and heat for remote sites. It outlines intended benefits, including long intervals between refueling and fewer specialist operators.
sources.cited_for: It supports the development goals of transportable nuclear power with a reduced operating burden.
sources.not_established: Design goals do not establish dependable service with little intervention across a complete installation’s lifetime.

sources.who: Los Alamos National Laboratory and NASA Glenn Research Center
sources.showed: The KRUSTY prototype space reactor adjusted its heat production to match demand from equipment that converted heat into electricity. It also tolerated the tested faults and changes in operating conditions.
sources.quote:
The key feature demonstrated was the ability of the reactor to
load-follow the demand of the power conversion system.
sources.cited_for: The test demonstrates integrated reactor operation and automatic adjustment to changing power demand.
sources.not_established: A short prototype test does not establish decades of remote service or the staffing and maintenance a deployed installation would need.

shown: Los Alamos National Laboratory and NASA Glenn Research Center ran the KRUSTY nuclear power system for 28 consecutive hours. This provides experimental progress toward dependable operation.
The Department of Energy describes designs intended to run for up to 10 years without refueling. That is a design goal; decades of dependable service with few visits remain to be demonstrated.
missing: Fuel, cooling, controls and supporting equipment must work together over the claimed lifetime, with their servicing needs established.
Safe operation during faults or lost communications must fit workable staffing, inspection, security and emergency-response arrangements.
Removal, transport and final handling of the system and its nuclear material need workable arrangements.

milestones.label: Remote operation establishes energy delivery and service needs
milestones.explanation: An independent remote-site trial would have to measure delivered energy, reliability, deterioration and every intervention under defined conditions. This would establish actual service, staffing and oversight needs.

milestones.label: Lifetime evidence supports claims beyond the trial
milestones.explanation: Longer lifetime claims would need field results linked to endurance tests, aging studies, fuel evidence and uncertainty estimates. This would address failures that a shorter trial could miss.

milestones.label: Independent assessment establishes practical support and final handling
milestones.explanation: An independent assessment would have to account for security, maintenance, recovery, lifetime costs and final handling, demonstrating removal or exchange where needed. This would establish the full support burden.

milestones.label: Open evaluation and repeated trials establish deployment range
milestones.explanation: Methods, performance data and intervention records would need independent scrutiny, with justified security restrictions, and trials across further units or sites. This would establish the range of conditions supported by testing.

uncertain: The required lifetime, useful power output, acceptable interruptions and allowable frequency of visits remain undefined.
How confidently a shorter trial can support a much longer service-life claim remains unresolved.
Whether the system would be economical depends on each site’s demand, transport constraints and support needs.

page.title: Nuclear microreactors with 20-year fuel cycles
page.definition: A transportable fission reactor and its power-conversion equipment supply 3–10 megawatts of electricity at a remote terrestrial site for a 20-year operating life without refuelling. This defines fuel autonomy; quantitative limits on staffing and maintenance remain unspecified.

goal.need: DOE identifies remote communities, mining, military installations and disaster relief as microreactor applications, noting that diesel generation in these markets can cost approximately US$600/MWh. Its proposed advantages include transportability, factory fabrication and longer intervals between refuelling.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy
statements.quote: A longer core life, operating for up to 10 years without refueling
operate continuously for 20 years, delivering 3-10 MWe of electricity with minimal maintenance requirements.
statements.context: The passage describes the XENITH design objective, not an operating result.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Defense, Defense Science Board
statements.quote: The first deployment of a vSMR prototype should be to a remote site
statements.context: vSMR denotes a very small modular reactor.

completion.title: A remote microreactor supplies 3–10 MWe for 20 years without refuelling.
completion.criterion: A complete transportable microreactor power system demonstrates the published XENITH objective at a remote terrestrial site: continuous electrical output within its declared 3–10 MWe specification over a 20-year operating life, without refuelling or core replacement. Actual electricity service is required. A calculated core lifetime or an operating authorisation alone does not satisfy this test. Staffing and maintenance are not graded because their published limits are unspecified.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, based on X-energy's prospectus dated April 23, 2026
completion.basis: DOE's microreactor objectives, the Defense Science Board report, Project Pele documentation, NRC's proposed Part 57 and developer specifications were searched for a combined duration, staffing, maintenance and availability acceptance test. None was found. This narrower test converts X-energy's explicit lifetime-fuel objective into an operating demonstration; it does not establish a quantified low-intervention capability.

milestones.title: A microreactor prototype passes an integrated non-nuclear system test.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the prototype's coupled heat-transfer and power-conversion systems without nuclear heat. NASA's Kilopower programme recognised this stage before nuclear system testing. Its presentation dated March 26, 2018 reports a successful non-nuclear system test of one KRUSTY prototype at Glenn Research Center; it supplies no numerical acceptance limits for that test.
milestones.set_by: NASA Kilopower programme, published test sequence for the KRUSTY space-power prototype
milestones.threshold_quote: Successful non-nuclear system test conducted at GRC.

milestones.title: A microreactor reaches initial criticality and passes low-power commissioning tests.
milestones.criterion: Establish a controlled, self-sustaining fission chain reaction and complete the applicable low-power tests, including shutdown-system availability, reactivity monitoring and agreement with the safety analysis. Partial results: DOE reported initial criticality of one Antares Mark-0 demonstrator on June 4, 2026; Westinghouse reported an eVinci critical experiment on August 24, 2026. Both announcements are not peer reviewed and establish initial criticality, not completion of all commissioning tests.
milestones.set_by: Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, REGDOC-2.3.1, section 11.3, Phase C; Canadian commissioning requirements
milestones.threshold_quote: During this phase, criticality of the fuel in the reactor core is achieved for the first time

milestones.title: A microreactor prototype completes a 28-hour integrated nuclear system test.
milestones.criterion: Complete the KRUSTY mission-profile test: startup, power increase, steady operation near a core temperature of 800 °C, reactor transients and shutdown within a 28-hour campaign. One KRUSTY space-reactor prototype completed 28 consecutive hours at varying power and temperature. The peer-reviewed report gives 1.5–5.0 kW of thermal power and demonstrates load-following of the electricity converters. This is a laboratory benchmark at kilowatt thermal scale.
milestones.set_by: NASA Kilopower programme, KRUSTY final-test protocol published in its March 26, 2018 advisory-council presentation; written for a space-power prototype
milestones.threshold_quote: Full Power test (28-hour full power test:

milestones.title: A transportable microreactor completes a three-year demonstration producing 1–5 MWe.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a transportable microreactor producing 1–5 megawatts of electricity on the Idaho National Laboratory microgrid and operating for at least three years, as specified for Project Pele. The cited DOE description does not define an availability percentage. DOE reported groundbreaking on September 24, 2024. An Army announcement dated December 3, 2025 reported the first fuel delivery; that announcement is not peer reviewed and does not establish operation.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Defense Strategic Capabilities Office, Project Pele objectives reported by DOE
milestones.threshold_quote: operate for a minimum of three years at the lab

milestones.title: A microreactor completes full-power commissioning at its remote operating site.
milestones.criterion: Complete staged commissioning through rated full power, demonstrating steady operation and the required responses to disturbances under the site's approved commissioning programme. CNSC Phase D supplies the commissioning test; the Defense Science Board supplies the remote-prototype deployment objective. The Air Force's March 2026 Eielson FAQ reports a notice of intent to award issued in May 2025, with licensing still required. It reports procurement progress, not commissioned operation.
milestones.set_by: Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, REGDOC-2.3.1, section 11.4, Phase D; remote siting follows the Defense Science Board's 2016 recommendation

not_found: No published operating record meeting the 20-year completion test was found.

results.finding: One KRUSTY prototype completed a 28-hour integrated nuclear system test.
results.detail: The campaign included startup, operation near 800°C, transients and shutdown. Thermal power ranged from 1.5 to 5.0 kW.
results.quote:
This paper presents results from the KRUSTY nuclear
system test, which operated the power system at various temperatures and power levels for 28 consecutive
hours.

results.finding: One electrically heated KRUSTY prototype produced 120 W from two Stirling converters.
results.detail: The depleted-uranium core simulator supplied nonfission heat through heat pipes to the converters; six thermal simulators represented the remaining conversion units.
results.quote:
Steady-state heat 
flow was determined to be acceptable to achieve 120 W of electrical power out of the two convertors.

results.finding: One KRUSTY test reactor completed 3 warm critical experiments.
results.detail: The tests demonstrated criticality, monitored reactivity and compared results with predictions. The text does not establish completion of all applicable low-power commissioning tests, including shutdown-system availability. KRUSTY was a 5-kW thermal space-reactor prototype.
results.quote:
These were followed by three
warm criticals, where fission power heated the core to 200°C, 300°C, and 450°C, respectively.

results.finding: One eVinci criticality test reached criticality at 663°C.
results.detail: The release reports a zero-power criticality experiment and a separate subcritical reactivity measurement. It does not establish completion of the applicable low-power commissioning tests.
results.quote: The Westinghouse eVinci™ microreactor test successfully reached zero-power high-temperature criticality at 663°C and a peak core temperature of 1,011°C, turning physics into evidence and accelerating the pathway to commercialization.

results.finding: One electrically heated KRUSTY system produced 120 W of electrical power from two Stirling converters.
results.detail: The test used a nonfissioning depleted-uranium core and simulated portions of the planned nuclear test. It did not demonstrate a 28-hour integrated nuclear campaign.
results.quote: Steady-state heat flow was determined to be acceptable to achieve 120 W of electrical power out of the two convertors.

results.finding: One KRUSTY prototype underwent a 6-hour nuclear warm-critical test.
results.detail: The test demonstrated passive reactor response before the full nuclear system test. The temperature was too low to thermally couple the power conversion system, and the 28-hour mission profile was not demonstrated in this test.
results.quote:
Figure 13 plots the 60 ¢ run on a much longer timescale,
which in this case is 6 h, to let the transient fully evolve.

results.finding: One Fission Surface Power demonstration unit produced 8.1 kW net in an integrated, non-nuclear system test.
results.detail: An electrically heated core simulator supplied a liquid-metal loop and Stirling power-conversion unit. The unit simulated one leg of the proposed system; a later helium breach ended testing.
results.quote:
When operated at the nominal operating conditions 
(modified for low liquid metal flow) during TDU testing the PCU produced 8.9 kW of power at an 
efficiency of 21.7 percent resulting in a net system power of 8.1 kW and a system level efficiency of 
17.2 percent.

results.finding: One KRUSTY reactor experiment underwent cold-critical reactivity measurements in 52 configurations.
results.detail: The experiments established criticality and measured reactivity. The paper does not establish completion of all applicable low-power commissioning tests, including shutdown-system availability and agreement with the safety analysis.
results.quote:
There were 52 configurations for the cold critical
experiments.

results.finding: One KRUSTY reactor core reached initial criticality on November 16, 2017.
results.detail: The ground demonstrator underwent cold and warm critical tests, but the paper does not establish completion of all specified commissioning checks, including shutdown-system availability and agreement with the safety analysis. It was a 1-kW-electric-class space-power demonstrator, below the entry’s 3–10-MW-electric target.
results.quote: The core went critical on November 16, 2017.
